8.

Let L be a lattice, show that C/L is a compact Riemann surface of genus 1.

解答.

解答.

∘

Let L=Zω1​⊕Zω2​ be the lattice, where ω1​,ω2​∈C are linearly independent on R, then the closed parallelogram P={aω1​+bω2​: a,b∈[0,1]} induces a projection P→C/L, thus L is compact. Hausdorff property and connectedness come easily from the property of P.

For each p∈C/L, choose z∈C with π(z)=p. π∣D(z,ε)​:D(z,ε)→U:=π(D(z,ε)) is a homeomorphism. Define a chart (U,φ), where φ=(π∣D(z,ε)​)−1.

Suppose (U1​,φ1​) and (U2​,φ2​) are two such charts with U1​∩U2​=∅. Let Vi​=φi​(Ui​). On a connected component of φ1​(U1​∩U2​), the composition φ2​∘φ1−1​ satisfiesπ(φ1−1​(z))=π(φ2−1​((φ2​∘φ1−1​)(z))),so φ1−1​(z)−φ2−1​((φ2​∘φ1−1​)(z))∈L. Since both points lie in small disks and L is discrete, this difference is constant on the component. Thus, φ2​∘φ1−1​ is a translation by a lattice element, hence holomorphic.

These charts form a holomorphic atlas, making C/L a Riemann surface.

∘

Secondly, we check it is of genus 1.

Because C/L≅P/{bω2​∼ω1​+bω2​,aω1​∼aω1​+ω2​}, we know C/L is homeomorphic to T2,

By the triangulation of T2 above, we have 2−2g(T2)=V+F−E=9+18−27=0⇒g(T2)=1.

□

9.

Let H∗=H∪{∞}, and π:H∗→X(1) be the projection, let D0​=21​π(i)+32​π(ρ)+π(∞)∈DivQ​(X(1)) be a Q-Cartier Divisor, prove that the map: M2k​(1)f​→{ω∈ΩX(1)k​:div(ω)≥−kD0​}↦ωf​=f(z)(dz)k​gives an isomorphism, conclude from it that M2k​≅O(kKX1​​+[kD0​]), then use Riemann-Roch Theory to calculate dimM2k​(1).

解答.

解答. We give a proof of the generalized case (where SL2​(Z) may be replaced by any congruence group Γ).

∘

First we know that weight-k modular form can be realized as a 2k​-holomorphic differential on the complete modular curve X(1), so the map M2k​(1)→ΩX(1)k​ is well-defined. We want to prove that there is an isomorphism: A2k​(Γ)→ΩX(Γ)k​, where A2k​ denotes the modular functions (only meromorphic needed).

The realization is given as follow:

For ω∈ΩX(Γ)k​, directly define the pullback of the natural projection

π:H→X(Γ),   π∗(ω)∈ΩHk​,

because H is an open subset of C, π∗(ω) can be written as f(z)(dz)k, where f is a global meromorphic function, and the transition compatibility

g∗(f(z)(dz)k)=f(z)(dz)k,∀g∈Γ

gives:

f(gz)=(cz+d)−2kf(z),

which means f is modular of weight-2k.

For f∈A2k​(Γ), we will construct a meromorphic differential ω(f)∈ΩX(Γ)k​ such that π∗(ω)=f(τ)(dτ)k. By the definition of meromorphic differentials it suffices to construct local differentials that pull back to restrictions of f(τ)(dτ)k. Thus the idea is to express f(τ)(dτ)k in local coordinates.

Each local map ψj​:Uj​⟶Vj​ is a composite ψj​=ρj​∘δj​:τ↦z↦q with δj​∈GL2​(C). Since δj​ is invertible it is easy to transform f(τ)(dτ)k into z-coordinates locally. First extend the weight-k operator [γ]k​ to matrices γ∈GL2​(C) by defining j(γ,τ)=cτ+d as we define on the SL2​(Z), and(f[γ]k​)(τ)=(detγ)k/2j(γ,τ)−kf(γ(τ))when this makes sense. Now let Uj′​=Uj​∩H. Then f(τ)(dτ)k∣Uj′​​ is a pullback δj∗​(λj​) where λj​ is the differential obtained by pulling f(τ)(dτ)k∣Uj′​​ forward to z-space under the change of multiplication by δj−1​. Letting α=δj−1​,λj​​=α∗(f(τ)(dτ)k∣Uj′​​)=f(α(z))(d(α(z)))k=(detα)kj(α,z)−2kf(α(z))(dz)k=(f[α]2k​)(z)(dz)k.​Thus λj​ is δj​Γδj−1​-invariant since f(τ)(dτ)k is Γ-invariant.

Denote rh​ the multiplication by μh​=eh2πi​.

When Uj​ does not contain a cusp, by δj​Γδj−1​-invariance, the pullback rh∗​(λj​)=(f[α]2k​)(μh​z)⋅μhk​(dz)k=λj​,Or equivalently, (μh​z)k(f[α]2k​)(μh​z)=zk(f[α]2k​)(z),

This shows that the function zl(f[α]2k​)(z) takes the form gj​(zh) for some meromorphic function g, and then we define:ωj​=(hq)kgj​(q)​(dq)k  on Vj​.(1)

When Uj​ contains a cusp, we similarly have the conclusion that f([α]2k​)(z) takes the form gj​(qh​), where h is the width and qh​=eh2πiz​, then we may define:ωj​=(2πiq/h)kgj​(q)​(dq)k  on Vj​.(2)

This finishes the construction of ω={ωj​}j∈J​. By tedious calculation we may see these two maps gives out a bijection.

Let τj​ be the center of Uj​, from (1) and (2) we know vπ(τj​)​(ω)​=v0​(qkgj​(q)​)=v0​(gj​)−k=h1​(vτj​​(f))+hn​−k=vπ(τj​)​(f)−k(1−h1​).​

So this means when f is a modular function (holomorphic), vπ(τj​)​(f)≥0, ∀τj​,

then vπ(τj​)​(ω)≥−k(1−h1​), then: M2k​(Γ)→{ω∈ΩX(Γ)k​:div(ω)≥−kD0​}

is an isomorphism.

∘

In the rest of the answer, we denote l(D)={f∈C(X(Γ)),f=0 or div(f)+D≥0}, then Riemann-Roch theorem says: dim(L(D))=deg(D)−g(X(Γ))+1+dim(L(div(λ)−D)), where λ is the canonical divisor.

Then we introduce a lemma:

引理 1.1 (lemma0.1).

(a) dim(L(div(λ)))=g.

(b) deg(div(λ))=2g−2.

(c) If deg(D)<0 then dim(L(D))=0.

(d) If deg(D)>2g−2 then dim(L(D))=deg(D)−g+1.

Proof of lemma0.1.

Note that dim(L(0))=1 , then we put D=0 into the Riemann-Roch Theorem, it turns out that 1=−g+1+dim(L(div(λ))), proving (a).

Next set D=div(λ), combine the Riemann-Roch Theorem with (a) to get g=deg(div(λ))−g+1+1, and (b) follows.

Further, suppose dim(L(D))>0. Then some nonzero f∈L(D) exists, so div(f)≥−D and taking degrees shows that deg(D)≥0, which is exactly (c).

Finally, (b) and (c) imply (d) since deg(D)>2g−2⇒deg(div(λ)−D)<0.

□

Back to the proof. We fix a modular function f0​∈A2k​, then M2k​={ff0​:f∈C(X(Γ)),div(ff0​)≥0}which leads to: M2k​={f∈C(X(Γ)),f≡0 or div(f)+div(f0​)≥0}=L([div(f0​)]).

By the discussion in the first question, if we pick ω∈ΩX(Γ)k​ corresponding to f0​, we know: [div(f)]=div(ω)+[2k​]i+[32k​]μ+k⋅∞.

By lemma we have div(ω)=2kg−2k, so deg([div(f)])=2k(g−1)+[2k​]+[32k​]+k≥2g−2.

Therefore by lemma,dim(M2k​)=(2k−1)(g−1)+[2k​]+[32k​]+k.

Put the geometric conclusion g=0 into it and classify by mod 6, we have:

dim(M2k​)=t+1, when  k=6t+0,2,3,4,5,dim(M2k​)=t, when  k=6t+1.

□

1.

Show that the cusps of the congruence group Γ0​(p) (p prime) are {0,∞}.

解答.

解答. For any ba​∈Q, gcd(a,b)=1,

if p∤b, then pick bc≡1 (mod p), we have [c0​ab​]⋅0=0+b0+a​=ba​ with [c0​ab​]∈Γ0​(p);

if p∣b, then p∤a, pick ac≡1 (mod p),[ab​0c​]⋅∞=ba​ with [ab​0c​]∈Γ0​(p).

解答.

命题 2.1. E2​(cz+daz+b​)=(cz+d)2E2​(z)+πi6c(cz+d)​.

5.

Show that dim(M4​(Γ0​(4)))=3.

解答.

解答. We know from Problem 4 that E4​(z)−4E4​(4z)∈M4​(Γ0​(4)), E4​(z)−2E4​(2z)∈M4​(Γ0​(2))⊆M4​(Γ0​(4)), E4​∈M4​(1)⊆M4​(Γ0​(4)),

and they are all linearly independent, so dim(M4​(Γ0​(4)))≥3,

On the other hand, we know that M4​(Γ0​(4)) does not contain nonzero cusp forms, which means:

if dim(M4​(Γ0​(4)))>3=#{Cusps of Γ0​(4)}, then there is a linear combination of these modular forms which gives out a cusp form, contradiction!

Therefore, dim(M4​(Γ0​(4)))=3.

6.

Show that dim(M2​(Γ0​(4)))=2. Further, E2,2​, E2,4​ is a basis.

证明.

证明.

Similar to the previous proof we have that dim(M2​(Γ0​(4)))≤3, and we know E2,2​,E2,4​∈M2​(Γ0​(4)) are linearly independent, now our goal is to prove that dim(M2​(Γ0​(4)))=3.

we may verify that Fi​∣γ​=fi​∣γ​+fi​∣αγ​+fi​∣βγ​=Fi​, ∀γ∈SL2​(Z), so Fi​=0 for there are no weight-2 modular form of SL2​(Z).

⎣⎡​f1​(0)f2​(0)f3​(0)​f1​(21​)f2​(21​)f3​(21​)​f1​(∞)f2​(∞)f3​(∞)​⎦⎤​⋅⎣⎡​A1​A2​A3​​⎦⎤​=0.

7.

Show that SL2​(Z)→SL2​(Z/NZ) is a surjective homomorphism.

解答.

解答. We only need to prove the surjectivity, pick γ=[ac​bd​]∈SL2​(Z/NZ), we know that gcd(a,c,N)=gcd(b,d,N)=1.

We know that γ can be decomposed into P1​⋯Pn​⋅[h0​0r​]⋅Q1​⋯Qm​, where P1​,⋯Pn​,Q1​,⋯Qm​ are elementary matrices, and every elementary matrix has a preimage of the form [1⋆​01​] or [10​⋆1​] or [01​10​] in SL2​(Z),

For the matrix [h0​0r​], we assume hr=tN+1, and uncertain [h+h′NgN​fNr+r′N​], then we need (h+h′N)(r+r′N)−gfN2=1.

Equivalently, N(h′r+r′h+N(h′r′−gf))=−tN.

Then because gcd(r,N)=gcd(h,N)=1, we may find h′,r′∈Z with h′r+r′h+t≡0 (mod N). then pick g,f∈Z, we have done!

8.

(1) Show that GL2​(Z/pZ) has order (p2−1)(p2−p).

(2) Show that SL2​(Z/pZ) has order (p2−1)p.

解答.

解答. (1)

This is equivalent to finding a basis of (Z/pZ)2, there are (p2−1) nonzero vectors in (Z/pZ)2 and (p2−p) vectors that are not collinear with the first one.

(2)

We first pick the first row of SL2​(Z/pZ), there are (p2−1) nonzero vectors, if one of the entries is zero, then the second row has one fixed entry and another free entry, which amount to p vectors;

if all the entries are nonzero, then we may pick any number in {0,1,⋯,p−1} be the third entry, and the forth entry is fixed, which means there are also p choices.

By multiplication principle, there are totally (p2−1)p matrices.

□

11.

Let f,g∈Sk​(1) be normalized eigenforms for all the Hecke operators, show that either ⟨f,g⟩SL2​(Z)​=0 or f=g.

解答.

解答. We will use two calculative facts proved in the class:

(1) Tp∗​=⟨p−1⟩Tp​;

(2) ⟨p⟩∗=⟨p−1⟩.

We denote λf,n​,λg,n​ the eigenvalue of Tn​ on f,g respectively, μf,n​,μg,n​ the eigenvalues of ⟨n⟩ on f,g respectively.

We assume that ⟨f,g⟩=L=0, then consider:λf,p​L=⟨Tp​f,g⟩=⟨f,⟨p−1⟩Tp​g⟩=λg,p​μg,p​​LWe get:λf,p​=λg,p​μg,p​​.

We know from Problem 12 that λf,p​∈R, by a classical conclusion we have: μp​ is an N-th unity, and when considering cusp forms of SL2​(Z), we have μp​=1.

So we get:λf,p​=λg,p​.(3)

For any n≥2, we prove by induction that λg,p​λf,p​​=⋯=λg,pn​λf,pn​​=s. By the formula Tpr​=Tp​Tpr−1​−pr−1⟨p⟩Tpr−2​, we have: λpr​=λp​λpr−1​−pr−1μp​λpr−2​.

This means:λf,pn​=λg,pn​μg,pn​​=λg,pn​(μg,p​)n​=λg,pn​.

Therefore f,g have exactly the same eigenvalues for all the Hecke operators and Diamond operators, therefore they are homothetic, also they are both normal forms, f=g.

解答. Let Mk​(Z) be the set of modular forms

f=n=0∑∞​c(n)qn

of weight k whose coefficients c(n) are integers. One can prove that there exists a Z-basis of Mk​(Z) which is a C-basis of Mk​. [More precisely, one can check that Mk​(Z) has the following basis (recall that F=q∏n=1∞​(1−qn)24):

k is of the form 4k: One takes the monomials E4α​Fβ where α,β∈N, and α+3β=2k​;

Also, Mk​(Z) is stable under T(n),n≥1. We conclude from this that the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of T(n). acting on Mk​, are integers, therefore the eigenvalues are algebraic integers.

Because Hecke operator Tp​ is self-adjoint in Petersson Inner Product, the eigenvalues are real.

Assume σ∈Gal(C/Q) maps an eigenvalue λ to σλ, we know that Hecke operators Tn​ are algebraic on the coefficients of the Fourier series, therefore fσ is an eigenform of eigenvalue σλ, therefore σλ∈R, which means λ is totally real.

5.

Let C(Γ0​(N)) be the field of modular functions for Γ0​(N). Show that C(Γ0​(N)) is generated by jN​(z) over C(j)=C(Γ(1)).

(Notice: “field of modular functions” means the function field of the modular curve X0​(N), or equivalently the modular functions of weight-0).

解答.

解答. We consider a homomorphism θ:SL2​(Z)→Aut(C(X0​(N)), γ↦(f↦f∘γ),

(i)

For any γ=[ac​bd​]∈SL2​(Z), we have: jN​(γ(τ))​=j(Nγτ)=j([aNc​​Nbd​]Nτ);​

Because j is a bijection between X(1) to C, if θ(γ)=id, then j(Nτ)=jN​(τ)=jN​(γτ)=j([aNc​​Nbd​]Nτ)

gives out Nτ=[aNc​​Nbd​](Nτ) in X(1), which means [aNc​​Nbd​]∈SL2​(Z), or equivalently, γ∈Γ0​(N).

Therefore, the fixing group of C(j,jN​) is Γ0​(N).

(ii)

We have already verified jN​∈C(Γ0​(N)), then C(j,jN​)⊆C(Γ0​(N)), by the reverse inclusion,kerθ={the fixing group of C(Γ0​(N))}⊆{the fixing group of C(j,jN​)}.

(iii)

Because the modular curve X0​(N)=H/Γ0​(N), Γ0​(N) acts trivially on X0​(N), therefore Γ0​(N)⊆kerθ.

(iv)

Combine (i),(ii),(iii), we know that all the ⊆ should be =. Then consider the fixing field C(X0​(N))SL2​(Z)/kerθ=C(j), by Galois Theory, C(X0​(N))/C(j) is a Galois extension with Galois group SL2​(Z)/kerθ=SL2​(Z)/Γ0​(N).

Similarly we have C(j,jN​)/C(j) is also Galois with Galois group SL2​(Z)/Γ0​(N), then by Galois correspondence C(j,jN​)=C(Γ0​(N)).

□

6.

Let Λ⊆C be a lattice, and let α∈C−Z, prove that ℘Λ​(αz) is a rational function of ℘Λ​(z) if and only if αΛ⊆Λ.

解答.

解答.

When ℘(αz) is a rational function of ℘(z), we know ℘(α(z+ω))=℘(α(z)) for any ω∈Γ, therefore αΛ⊆Λ.

For the reverse, since ℘(αz) is Λ/α-periodic and also Λ-periodic, ℘(αz) can be lifted to a function in C/Λ, and hence in the function field Γ(C/Λ)=C(℘)[℘′]/(℘′2−(4℘3−A℘−B)).

So we may write ℘(αz) in the form c1​+c2​℘′+g(℘)f(℘)​, where f,g are rational functions. Because ℘(αz) is even, and ℘ is even, ℘′ is odd, there should not be c2​℘′ in the denominator, thus is ℘(αz) a rational funtion of ℘(z).

□
